# Introduction

Here is a basic discussion of regression trees. A good source for this topic is from the [University of Cincinnati](#r1), which has a good business analytics program. Another good one is from [Datacamp](#r2). The basic reference on tree modeling is [Breiman et al., 1984](#r3).

Decision Trees work by recursively partitioning the data one variable at a time. Predictions are obtained by finding out which leaf of the tree an observation comes out in; the mean value of the target in that leaf is assigned as the prediction. 

The interpretation of a decision tree is easy, though perhaps not as easy as a linear regression. But it has a lot of intuition behind it. Of course data scientists have carried the concept to extremes, designing more complicated variations. And those are correspondingly less explainable.

[Our text](#r4) gives a good discussion of decision trees and their variations. However, this notebook does not follow the book. It's even simpler.

# Packages

As usual, we have some standard packages. Code for regression trees can be found in the packages `rpart, rpart.plot` which you must load.

```{r}
library(ISLR2)
library(rpart) # for decision trees
library(rpart.plot) # plotting decision trees
library(mbadtools, quietly=TRUE) # some extra ggplot functions
```

# Data

Load the advertising data. It's in a csv file from early in the course. You can use Import Dataset.

```{r}
Advertising <- read_csv("Advertising.csv")
```

# Data Description

Give the data a short df name.

```{r}
data = Advertising
data
```

The first column has a strange name. It numbers the Ad Campaigns studied. Sales is considered to be the target variable. the others are the drivers, the amount invested in the types of advertising for the campaign.

# Data Wrangling
We change the name of the first column.
```{r}
data = data %>% rename(Campaign=1)
data %>% glimpse
```

# Research Problem
We will build a regression tree to model the prediction of Sales from the other variables. This is a supervised method. We will compare the result with a linear model.

# Method
We will use a simple regression tree.
To build the tree we will use the `rpart` function from the package of the same name.  

# Set a seed
Since it does some randomization we set a seed so the notebook will reproduce.
```{r}
set.seed(1)
```

# Calculate Regression Tree
We want a regression tree so we set 'method' to "anova".

```{r}
tree.rpart <- rpart(
  formula = Sales~TV+Radio+Newspaper,
  data    = data,
  method  = "anova" #this is for regression tree
)
```

# Summarize result

The summary tells you what happened at each step of the construction, and much else.

```{r}
summary(tree.rpart)
```

# Visualize the tree
There are various types of plots. The default is type=2.
```{r}
rpart.plot(tree.rpart) # default type is 2
```
More types of plot.
```{r}
rpart.plot(tree.rpart, type=4)
rpart.plot(tree.rpart, type=5)
```


The numbers at the bottom are the mean values of Sales in the various tree classes. The percentages are the percentages of cases that fall there.

# Predictions

```{r}
tree.prediction=predict(tree.rpart,data)
ggplot(data, aes(1:nrow(data), Sales)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(aes(1:nrow(data), tree.prediction), color="red", shape=5)
```

# Calculate mean average percentage error (MAPE)

```{r}
tree.prediction.error = sum(abs(tree.prediction - data$Sales))/sum(data$Sales)
tree.prediction.error
```

```{r}
plotcp(tree.rpart)
```

You can see that the relative error declines till a cp value of about .04, then levels off.

# Linear Regression
Now we do a linear regression on all drivers for comparison and report the MAPE of the predictions on the dataset.

```{r}
model1 = lm(Sales ~ TV + Radio + Newspaper, data)
model1.prediction = predict(model1, data )
model1.prediction.error = sum(abs(model1.prediction - data$Sales))/sum(data$Sales)
model1.prediction.error
```

# Conclusion
Tree prediction error is a bit less than ordinary regression prediction error. You'll get a different answer if you rerun the tree with a different seed.

```{r}
data.frame(MAPE.linear = model1.prediction.error, 
           MAPE.tree = tree.prediction.error)
```
